card.hook: Here's a cheeky trick: on a still day, Brosundet gives you two towns for the price of one, because the water can copy the buildings upside down. If it's rippled, don't sulk. Boats and buildings still make a lovely picture.
card.stand_here: Stand about 35 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. That gives you the whole canal scene in front of you, with water, buildings and boats.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the canal. If you're close to the water and want more in the frame, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for details that catch your eye.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edge of the water or a row of buildings with one of the horizontal lines, so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day is flattering. Pick a still day if you want the best reflections.
card.selfie_here: Try the waterside by Apotekergata, along the quay where Apotekergata meets the canal, next to the statues on the waterfront. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold the phone slightly out and up so the pastel buildings fill the space behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Hellebroa bridge to shoot you with the Brosundet canal in the background.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole scene, then hunt for three little details, such as a boat, a window or a reflection, and pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Brosundet is a canal in Ålesund, and it's the first stop on this map. Water, buildings and boats make natural subjects for a simple picture. Ripples break up the reflections, so take a couple of frames a few seconds apart and keep the best one.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 35 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. That gives you the whole canal scene in front of you, with water, buildings and boats.

selfie_research.safety: Wear comfortable walking shoes, since the path up Aksla's 418 steps can be steep in places (a viewpoint guide; this refers to the Aksla climb, not the canal).
selfie_research.notes: No page gave a precise photographer position for the ask-someone shot; the Hellebroa bridge entry is a general 'photo stop with a view of Brosundet'. The Apotekergata spot is taken from a review, and the statues there are not named. No page mentioned selfie-stick or tripod rules for Brosundet, so none are reported. Fjellstua viewpoint on Aksla was left out because its view shows the canal below rather than behind the visitor.

card.hook: You've made it up Mount Aksla, and the Fjellstua restaurant is right there, with the whole view behind you waiting for its turn. Photograph the building first, then spin around and let the landscape have its moment.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 10 m west of the subject at Fjellstua viewpoint, and face east to photograph the Fjellstua building. Then turn around to take in the view.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x for the big wide scene, then use 1x for the Fjellstua building. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single detail in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, then tap your main subject and drag the slider down a little if the sky looks too bright.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or evening usually gives softer light, but any clear time of day works. Check the weather before you set out, because cloud can hide the view.
card.selfie_here: Try the white park bench at the top, a few metres up from the Fjellstua restaurant's parking area. It looks out over the town and bay, so it makes a nice seated selfie. For a quieter option, walk on to Kniven viewpoint. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and check that the town is behind your shoulder before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the front of the Fjellstua restaurant building at the top and ask a passer-by to frame you with the building and the town below.
card.rules_and_safety: The path up Aksla can be steep in places, so wear sturdy shoes. Check the official site for current access to the viewpoint and the restaurant.
card.challenge: Walk a little way along the viewing area and find the spot where no railing or sign sneaks into your shot.
card.good_to_know: Fjellstua is a viewpoint on Mount Aksla, ranked second on the Ålesund map. The map marks the Fjellstua restaurant right at the viewpoint. Local transport isn't listed for this spot, so check your options for getting to Mount Aksla before you set out.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 10 m west of the subject at Fjellstua viewpoint, and face east to photograph the Fjellstua building. Then turn around to take in the view.

selfie_spots.detail: the smaller lookout on the Aksla ridge, reached by paths beyond the main Fjellstua terrace
selfie_spots.why: Guides describe it as a quieter lookout with different angles on the town, so it suits a selfie with the town and mountain behind you.

card.hook: Most aquarium photos are a seal behind scratched glass with your own reflection in it. Here the seals swim in an open-air pool, with a fjord and mountains behind them, so you get the whole scene with no glass in the way.
card.stand_here: Go to the outdoor seal pool area (Selbukta) and stand about 20 m east of the numbered pin. Face west, with the pool in front of you and the fjord and peaks beyond it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the big picture of seals with the fjord and peaks behind. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a close-up of a seal or otter at the pool edge. Zoom 0.5x works for the open sea and rocky shoreline, but keep faces away from the edges of the frame or they stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the animal, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky and mountains keep their detail, and use the gridlines to keep the horizon level.
card.best_time: Pick a bright, clear day so the mountains show up behind the pool. Check the official site for show and feeding times.
card.selfie_here: Hold your phone at arm's length with the front camera, and switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it so more of the scene fits in. Keep something big and recognisable over your shoulder and take a few frames, because the background will be moving.
card.rules_and_safety: Paths around Tueneset can be uneven and rocky, so wear sturdy walking shoes. It's a ticketed aquarium, so check the official site for entry rules and photo guidance, and turn your flash off because it may be restricted in some areas.
card.challenge: Seals never sit still, so take a burst of shots and see if you can catch one mid-swim with the peaks lined up behind it and the horizon dead level.
card.good_to_know: Atlanterhavsparken was founded in 1951, and the current building opened on 15 June 1998, during Ålesund's 150th anniversary. The open-air seal pool, Selbukta, opened in 2014 and holds around 15 million litres of water, which makes it one of the largest seal exhibits in the world. It's home to harbour seals.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the outdoor seal pool area (Selbukta) and stand about 20 m east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map. Face west, with the pool in front of you and the fjord and peaks beyond it.

selfie_research.safety: Paths around Tueneset can be uneven and rocky, so sturdy walking shoes are recommended. Sources: Tueneset Ålesund (airial.travel); 15 Things to Do in Alesund (daytripsfrom.city).
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific spot where a visitor can take a selfie with the Atlanterhavsparken aquarium behind them, and none names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole building in frame. I have not added any place from memory, so selfie_spots and ask_someone_spot are empty. Pages that mention the site describe the outdoor seal and penguin areas with good natural light (Atlanterhavsparken Café listing on airial.travel), the open-air coastal zone facing the ocean (visitnorway.nl), and the rocky Tueneset coastal paths (Norway Explained). These are useful for photos but do not place the aquarium behind a person. Mount Aksla is named as a viewpoint (Norway Explained, Fodor's), but its pages describe views over the town, not the aquarium. Tripadvisor photo listings had no usable location detail. On equipment, Norway Explained says tripods are impractical at the outdoor area and suggests a beanbag or jacket on a railing; this is advice, not a rule, so I have not listed it under rules. Norway Explained also advises against flash because it stresses animals, but that concerns photography generally, not selfie sticks or tripods, so I have left it out. Practical sources: Norway Explained (norwayexplained.com/atlanterhavsparken/), airial.travel Atlanterhavsparken Café and Tueneset pages, visitnorway.nl listing, fodors.com Ålesund sights, daytripsfrom.city. A local check on arrival, or asking the aquarium staff about photo spots, would likely resolve this.

card.hook: Picture sod-roofed farmhouses, a little lake and mountains in the background, and hardly anyone else around. Down at the quay, replica boats are waiting to be in your photos too.
card.stand_here: Stand in Borgundgavlen, on the open ground among the old houses near the small lake. You'll be about 540 m south-west of the subject, so face north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the wide view of farmhouses, fjord and mountains. Try 0.5x if you want more sky and lake. At the quay, zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) picks out the boat halls and replica boats.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower line, and use an old house as your foreground.
card.best_time: Morning light gives a soft, dreamy look. Going away from the busiest times also means fewer people in your shots.
card.selfie_here: Head to the lakeside by the Fjordmannstova hut, the fishermen's shelter beside the small lake. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the hut and the water over your shoulder. Some of the buildings are reflected in a pond, which makes a pretty backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the shore of Nørvasundet, the strait next to the museum, where the boat halls are photographed from, and pose with the boat halls behind you (check it works on the spot).
card.rules_and_safety: The churchyard at Borgund kyrkje is still an active cemetery, so keep a respectful distance and keep graves and people out of the frame. Paths can be icy and many outdoor buildings may be closed in winter, so check conditions after snowfall. We couldn't confirm whether the grounds and quay need a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Frame one old house as your foreground with the lake and mountains behind it, then walk to the quay and get a replica boat in the shot too.
card.good_to_know: Sunnmøre Museum is an open-air museum of old buildings on the peninsula around Borgundgavlen. Down by the quay you'll find replicas of the Borgundknarren and the Kvalsundskipet in front of the boat halls. For a different view, walk to Borgund kyrkje, which shows the museum's buildings from the south.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Borgundgavlen, on the open ground among the old houses near the small lake (the phone icon on the map). You'll be about 540 m south-west of the subject, so face north-east.

The ask-someone spot is inferred from a Wikimedia photo caption that says the boat halls were photographed from Nørvasundet; no page says a passer-by should stand there, so verify on the ground. card.hook: Picture a tiny red-and-white tower at the end of a canal, with bobbing boats in front and pastel warehouses on both sides. Now picture sleeping in it, because Molja Lighthouse is actually a hotel room.
card.stand_here: Stand on Brosundet, about 240 m south-east of the subject, and face north-west. The lighthouse sits at the far end of the water, with moored boats and the warehouses lining the canal.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the lighthouse framed by the boats and warehouses. Try 0.5x for more canal and reflections, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer without walking onto the pier.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the lighthouse, then slide the brightness down a touch so the white and red don't wash out and the reflections keep their colour.
card.best_time: Calm mornings are best, when the water is still enough for clear reflections and the canal is quieter. In the evening, switch on night mode and rest your phone on a rail or wall to keep it steady, and expect a lit hotel window.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tuck the lighthouse over your shoulder so it fits behind you. Hold the phone a bit higher and tilt it slightly up to get more of the tower in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand well back on the stone breakwater so the whole tower fits in the frame, while you pose with the lighthouse behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The walkway is public, but the lighthouse is part of a hotel, so check the official site if you hope to go inside. The pier is afloat and boats are usually anchored there, so watch your step and take extra care in icy or stormy weather.
card.challenge: Can you catch the lighthouse upside-down in the water, with one boat sitting neatly in the corner of your shot?
card.good_to_know: Molja Lighthouse stands at the mouth of the Brosundet canal, on the edge of Ålesund's harbour. It's run by Hotel Brosundet as a hotel room, so it's a working building, not just a monument. The warehouses along the quay date from the early 1900s, and you might see a light on in the lighthouse in the evening.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Brosundet (the phone icon on the map), about 240 m south-east of the subject, and face north-west. The lighthouse sits at the far end of the water, with moored boats and the warehouses lining the canal.

ask_someone_spot.name: Molja breakwater (the stone walkway out to the lighthouse), standing well back from the tower
ask_someone_spot.detail: On the breakwater, a good distance back from the lighthouse so the whole tower fits in frame. The sources advise shooting from further back on the breakwater with a wide lens, and note the lighthouse is a fair distance away, so a telephoto-style framing may be needed. The exact standing point is my inference from these tips, not a named spot.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found places a visitor with the lighthouse directly behind them, so I left selfie_spots empty rather than guess. The closest is Aksla Viewpoint, where a photographer frames the harbour with Molja Fyr 'visible at the edge' (Pixeo), which is not a selfie-with-lighthouse-behind setup, and it is not a spot where a passer-by would shoot the whole landmark. The 'ask someone' spot is an inference from advice aimed at photographers, so confirm the exact standing point on the ground. Sources disagree on the build year (1855 in Evendo, 1858 in several others). Some sources say the lighthouse is a hotel room (Room 47 at Hotel Brosundet), so the interior may be occupied; no page reports a ban on photographing from the outside.

card.hook: Nearly the whole town burned down in 1904, and this pale marble church is part of what rose from the ashes. The tower sits off to one side, so even a quick snap looks unmistakably like Ålesund.
card.stand_here: Stand right in front of Ålesund Church on Aspøya, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the church so the whole building fits in your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because you're close to a big building. Hold the phone level and leave a little space above the roof so the walls don't lean. Then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, and 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out the tower or the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the church's straight edges with them, then tap the church and drag the slider to make it a little darker if the sky is bright, so the pale stone doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Daylight is best, so you can see the stonework. On a bright day, try morning or early evening when the light is softer, and check which side of the church is catching the sun.
card.selfie_here: Try the church grounds on the garden side (Aspegata 9), on the lawns beside the church. Use the front camera at 0.5x and stand with the church over your shoulder. No exact selfie spot is marked there, so have a look around the lawns and pick the angle that shows the most church.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the church grounds on the Prestegata side, facing the façade, while you stand in front of the church so the whole front fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the church, flash is generally discouraged to protect the artwork, so check the signs or ask staff about photos. It's a working place of worship, so check the official site or the parish for visiting times and dress expectations before you go in.
card.challenge: Take a matching pair: one wide shot of the whole church, then one close-up of the marble and tower, and see if you can get both with perfectly straight walls.
card.good_to_know: Sverre Knudsen designed the church in the Art Nouveau style, and it was finished in 1909. The earlier church on this site was destroyed in the great fire of 23 January 1904. King Haakon VII laid the foundation stone in 1906, and roughly 2,000 square metres of marble cover the façade.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right in front of Ålesund Church on Aspøya, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the church so the whole building fits in your screen.

selfie_spots.why: A guide describes a well-kept garden around the church and suggests views of the church against the town's backdrop, which points to the grounds as the setting for a shot with the church behind you.

card.hook: Picture a layer cake: grass or rock at your feet, a stretch of open space, then the town, then sky and maybe some hills. That's the view from Slinningsodden, and your phone loves it because the layers do the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand about 580 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. That points you at the Slinningsodden town view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the whole scene. Then try 0.5x if you want more foreground and sky, or 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out a cluster of buildings.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third line if the sky is the star, or the upper third line if the town is.
card.best_time: Pick a clear spell, ideally in the softer light of morning or late afternoon. Dusk is worth a go too: use night mode and tuck your elbows in.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, try 0.5x, and turn so the town sits over your shoulder. Check the horizon behind you isn't sloping before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site or local tourist information before you go to find out whether this spot is open or restricted.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one zoomed shot of the same scene, then pick your favourite later and see if you chose the same one as your travel buddy.
card.good_to_know: The bonfire is built on a small island by Slinningsodden, on the Hessa peninsula in Ålesund. Weather can change quickly here, so check the sky before you set out. Wipe your phone's camera too, because fingerprints soften distant views.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 580 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. That points you at the Slinningsodden town view.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot on Slinningsodden with the town behind the visitor, and none names a passer-by spot that frames the visitor with the whole landmark, so I have left both empty rather than guess. What the pages do say: <cite index="15-4">The bonfire is built on a small island by Slinningsodden, located on the Hessa peninsula in Ålesund.</cite> <cite index="15-5">You can see it from many places around town, for example from the south side of the town centre at Volsdalsberga (near the football stadium), or from Mount Aksla.</cite> Mount Aksla is the town-view spot the pages describe most, with <cite index="6-7">the almost 270-degree view from the terrace at the top of the hill</cite>, but no page links that terrace to Slinningsodden as a backdrop. A tour page also names Hellebroa Bridge as a selfie stop, but it does not connect it to Slinningsodden either. Slinningsodden's own listing puts its GPS point at 62.46246, 6.16869, close to your position. A field check on the ground would be needed to find a spot that frames the town from Slinningsodden.

card.hook: Alnes Lighthouse is a tall white tower with nothing around it to clutter the frame, just open sky and sea. It's also one of the most visited lighthouses in Norway, so expect a few strangers to wander through your shot.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 40 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east. The lighthouse sits in front of you with room for sky above it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole tower with sky around it. Step closer and try 0.5x for a second shot, or go to 2x or more for a tighter picture of the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines instead of dead centre, and keep your phone level so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or evening is often kinder than the middle of the day. If you also want to go inside, aim for May to October, when the tower is open.
card.selfie_here: Head down to the rocky shore below the lighthouse, on the rocks along the shore beside the tower, and turn so the lighthouse is behind you at sunset. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x to fit more of the tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At the Alnes view point, which looks over the village, the lighthouse sits in the middle of the frame with houses around it, mountains on one side and open sea on the other, so ask someone to take your photo there (check a map to find it).
card.rules_and_safety: Reviewers say the tower's steps are steep and narrow, so wear good footwear. Some people climb down backwards. If you plan to go inside the tower or museum, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get one shot with the tower upright on a gridline and sky above it, then one with you in the rocks and the lighthouse standing guard behind you.
card.good_to_know: A light was first established here in 1852 to guide fishing boats into the harbour, and the tower you see today dates from 1876. It's still in operation, was automated in 1982 and is now owned by Giske Municipality. The old keeper's house has a café and an exhibition hall, and there's a small museum inside the tower.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 40 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east. The lighthouse sits in front of you with room for sky above it.

card.hook: Here's the surprise: this is a marble church, but it's been painted white with chalk, so you'll have to hunt for the actual marble. What you get is a plain, pale little building that really pops against the sky.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 10 m south-west of Giske Church, and face north-east. That puts the whole church in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which should fit the whole church from where you stand. Go to 0.5x if you want more sky and grass around it, and try 2x or higher for windows, doorways and wall texture.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white wall, then drag the slider to make it a touch darker so the walls keep their texture instead of turning flat white.
card.best_time: A bright but slightly hazy day works well, and so does the softer light of morning or evening. Harsh midday sun can wash out the detail on those white walls.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x so more of the church fits in. Turn so the church sits over your shoulder, and step back a bit if the walls look cut off.
card.rules_and_safety: You can only go inside on guided tours, which run in summer. Check the official site before you go if you hope to see the interior.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and take one shot where the walls sit perfectly straight, then see if you can spot a patch where the marble shows through the chalk.
card.good_to_know: Giske Church dates from the 12th century and began as a family chapel for the noble Giske family. It was renovated after 1756, and most of the interior comes from that work. Larger windows were added in the 1860s, and today it seats about 125 people.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 10 m south-west of Giske Church, and face north-east. That puts the whole church in front of you.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with Giske Church behind the visitor, or a named spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole church. Sources only say the exterior is good for photos without naming a position: Viking Sagaen (https://www.vikingisland.no/en/about-4) recommends photographing the exterior, and Tripadvisor reviews (https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g190504-d5995323-Reviews-Giske_Kirke-Alesund_More_og_Romsdal_Western_Norway.html) mention good photo opportunities outside the church without locating them. The Pilegrimsleden page (https://www.pilegrimsleden.no/en/interest-points/giske) describes a trail from the parking area by the bridge to the church, but gives no photo position. Other points: the church is on Giske island about 10 km from Ålesund city, not inside the city. Sources give conflicting build dates (c. 1130, 1150, 1170). Most of the marble is covered by chalk or plaster, so the marble shows only in a few places on the exterior. The interior is open for guided tours mainly in summer, and SeaDream's tour describes the photo stop as exterior only (https://seadream.com/voyages/landadventure/2111). The Pilegrimsleden page also mentions kissing crosses carved on the outside of the eastern wall, which may be worth a look but is not a selfie spot. Sources should be checked on site before a spot is added to the map.

card.hook: Here's a fun twist: you're about to photograph a former pharmacy that's far fancier than any chemist you've ever queued in. The Swan Pharmacy fills your frame nicely, ornament and all.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 45 m east of the subject, and face west toward Jugendstilsenteret. From here the whole building fits in one shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole façade. Use 0.5x only if you're so close that the building won't fit. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out ornament and details higher up.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Go when the sun is on the front of the building. Since you're facing west, that's usually morning to early afternoon. On a cloudy day the soft, even light is lovely for the detail shots.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement on Apotekergata in front of the Swan Pharmacy at No. 16, with the building right behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt up a little so the building rises over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: If you go inside, check the official site first, because photography rules can differ between rooms and exhibitions.
card.challenge: Take one full-building shot with dead-straight walls, then find one little decoration up high and make it the star of its own photo.
card.good_to_know: The building was the Swan Pharmacy (Svaneapoteket), designed by Hagbarth Martin Schytte-Berg and built between 1905 and 1907. In 1984 it became the first listed Art Nouveau monument in the town, and it still has the best preserved Art Nouveau interior in Ålesund. The centre opened in 2003, with Queen Sonja of Norway performing the opening.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 45 m east of the subject, and face west toward Jugendstilsenteret. From here the whole building fits in one shot.

card.hook: Nobody comes to Skateflukaia for one famous thing, and that's the fun of it. Boats bob, the quay curves off, buildings line up behind, and you get to decide what the picture is about.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Skateflukaia waterfront at the phone icon on the map, about 65 m west of the subject, and face east. That's enough distance to fit the water, the quay and the buildings in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole waterfront. Switch to 0.5x if you want more of the surroundings, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details like boats or reflections.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and keep the phone level so the horizon and quay edges look straight, and if the sky looks washed out, tap the water or buildings and drag the slider to make the picture a touch darker.
card.best_time: Soft morning or evening light is kinder to water and buildings. A calm day gives you the best reflections, so check the weather before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the benches in the small park beside the harbour basin, where the Englandsfarten monument stands. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the water behind your shoulder, and check the screen to see whether the monument fits, because we couldn't confirm an exact spot for it.
card.rules_and_safety: It looks like an open waterfront area, but check local signs in case any part is restricted.
card.challenge: Take three shots in a row: one wide, one close-up of a rope, railing or boat, and one with calm water filling the bottom of the frame.
card.good_to_know: Skateflukaia is a place for atmosphere rather than one single famous object. You may see boats, reflections, the quay and buildings all together. If people walk through your shot, wait a moment for a cleaner one.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Skateflukaia waterfront at the phone icon on the map, about 65 m west of the subject, and face east. That's enough distance to fit the water, the quay and the buildings in one frame.

card.hook: A bronze Fisher Boy on the water's edge, Art Nouveau buildings behind him, and you with a phone in your hand. That's a pretty good five-minute stop.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map at Apotekertorget, then turn to the north-west. You'll be looking straight at the spot. The text gives no stand-here distance, so just follow the icon.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the whole square. If buildings get cut off at the edges, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x (or higher, depending on your phone) to pick out one detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building edges with the vertical lines so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can make harsh shadows, so check the shot on screen and tweak it if needed.
card.selfie_here: Go to the Fiskergutten (Fisher Boy) statue on the square, right on the bank of Ålesundet. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone so the statue and the Art Nouveau buildings fit over your shoulder. For a different shot, stand beside the Sildekona (Herring Wife) statue in the middle of the square, near the harbour steps, and let the open square sit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Visitors say there are bird droppings almost everywhere around the Fiskergutten statue, so watch where you put your hands and feet when you pose.
card.challenge: Get the Fisher Boy, the water and at least one fancy building all in one frame, with zero seagull photobombs.
card.good_to_know: Apotekertorget's name suggests a town square, and it works well as a relaxed stop on a walk around Ålesund. The Fiskergutten statue stands right on the bank of Ålesundet (the sound). No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so use the map and the Navigate buttons to get there.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map at Apotekertorget, then turn to the north-west. You'll be looking straight at the spot. The text gives no stand-here distance, so just follow the icon.

selfie_spots.why: The statue sits on the square's waterfront edge, and the square is described as ringed by attractive buildings, so the statue and the surrounding architecture can both fit in a selfie.

card.hook: Nothing ruins a nice statue photo like a bin sprouting out of its head. Here, a few steps left or right sorts that out before you press the button.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 25 m north-west of the Kaiser Wilhelm statue in Byparken, and face south-east. From there you can see whether the statue and its surroundings fit in one shot, with a bit of breathing room around them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the statue and its setting together. Tap 2x if you want it a bit closer without walking over. Use 0.5x only when you're up close and want the surroundings in too.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the statue on a vertical line instead of dead centre, then keep the phone level so the paths and buildings behind don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when softer light shows off the shape of the statue. Midday sun makes harsh shadows and bright patches, but a cloudy day gives you even light and lots of detail.
card.selfie_here: Head to the small terrace beside the monument in Byparken and stand in front of the obelisk with the monument behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if you want more of the park in the frame.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few metres west of the obelisk, pointing the phone east so the whole monument fits, while you pose beside it (that spot is approximate, so adjust on the ground).
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one close-up, and see if you can get both without a single stranger or bin sneaking in.
card.good_to_know: This spot is ranked 13 on the Ålesund map. Different guides call the monument a statue, obelisk or memorial column. One describes it as a seven-metre obelisk with a relief of the emperor's profile.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 25 m north-west of the Kaiser Wilhelm statue in Byparken, and face south-east. From there you can see whether the statue and its surroundings fit in one shot, with a bit of breathing room around them.

Treat the 'ask someone' spot as approximate and check it on the ground. The position you gave (62.47333, 6.16118) is roughly 80 m south of the monument's coordinates on Wikimedia, so it may be near the park entrance rather than the monument itself. No page I found mentions selfie-stick or tripod rules, or a safety point for this spot. The 418 steps to Aksla are not wheelchair accessible, per one guide, but that is an accessibility note, not a safety point.

card.hook: Look up. On Kongens gate, the best stuff is way above the shop doors, where towers, windows and curly ornament are all fighting for your attention. One frame can hold the lot, and that makes it easy.
card.stand_here: Start on Kongens gate at the phone icon, about 200 m south of the subject, and face north so you can see how the buildings sit together. Then walk about 3 minutes towards them for your closer shots.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole street. If the facades are too tall to fit, drop to 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details high up on the buildings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the buildings with the vertical lines so they don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft daylight, like morning or late afternoon, usually shows off the ornament best. Overcast days work too, because the colours stay even and you avoid harsh shadows.
card.selfie_here: Stand on Kongens gate in front of house number 25, on the opposite side of the street from number 28, with the passageway and its Norse-style motifs behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and tilt up a little so the facade fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by near house number 18 on Kongens gate and ask for one upright shot with the facade filling the frame behind you.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole street, then hunt for three details up high that you'd never spot from the pavement: a tower, a window and a curl of ornament.
card.good_to_know: The facade of Kongens gate 25 is the only part of that building that survived a 1970 fire. Its passageway has Old Norse-inspired decoration. Directly across, number 28 (look for 'Bjørknes Skole' on the front) is Central European-style Art Nouveau, so you can see two very different styles in one view.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start on Kongens gate at the phone icon, about 200 m south of the subject, and face north so you can see how the buildings sit together. Then walk about 3 minutes towards them for your closer shots.

card.hook: Pale stone walls, a timber roof and tower, and a lawn dotted with old gravestones: Borgund Church looks good before you've even lifted your phone. And no, it's not a stave church, even though the wooden bits might make you think so.
card.stand_here: Head for the approach path at the front of the churchyard and step back along it, so you're facing the church with the whole building in front of you. The phone icon on the map marks the church itself, so stand back from it, not right at it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from the path to fit the whole church in. If you're close and the tower is getting chopped off, tap 0.5x. Zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) is great for the tower, the roof and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the church, then slide the brightness down a touch so the white walls keep their detail instead of going flat.
card.best_time: A bright overcast day is ideal, because the soft light is kind to white walls. Early morning or late afternoon gives you gentler light and fewer people in the churchyard.
card.selfie_here: Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone slightly high so the white church and tower sit over your shoulder. Check the tower isn't growing out of your head before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working church with a cemetery, so walk slowly and keep your voice down. Interior visits need to be arranged in advance, and photography inside may be restricted.
card.challenge: Take two shots of the church: one wide from the path, then one crouched low among the gravestones with a stone or two in the foreground. Which one would you frame?
card.good_to_know: The church goes back to around 1300 and mixes Romanesque and Gothic styles. A fire in 1904 destroyed most of it, but the medieval walls survived, and it was rebuilt inside them and consecrated in 1907. In 1814 it was also one of the polling stations for Norway's first national elections.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the approach path at the front of the churchyard and step back along it, so you're facing the church with the whole building in front of you. The phone icon on the map marks the church itself, so stand back from it, not right at it.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot or a passer-by photo spot for Borgund Church in Ålesund (62.46627, 6.2339), so both fields are empty rather than guessed. Church coordinates match Mapcarta (https://mapcarta.com/W388713713) and Wikidata (https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q11961968). The church sits on the Borgund peninsula next to Sunnmøre Museum and Borgundgavlen (https://www.wikiwand.com/no/articles/Borgund_kirke_(%C3%85lesund)). Pages on the Borgund Stave Church (Lærdal, c. 1180, dragon-head roofs, e.g. https://trips.klarna.com/en/adp/norway/alesund/borgund-church-a1132692391/ and https://www.airial.travel/attractions/norway/borgund-church-%C3%A5lesund-ayo7XFGW) describe a different building about 400 km away, so I excluded their photo tips, the 'graveyard' angle and the photography rules. The only viewpoint I found, on the walking loop from Borgundgavlen parking (https://www.westcoastpeaks.com/Peaks/borgundgavlen.html), has a view towards Ålesund, so the church would not be behind a visitor there. Sunnmøre Museum archive postcards show the church seen through an avenue of trees and the church from Borgundgavlen across Katavågen (https://digitaltmuseum.no/021015900667/aalesund-borgund-kirke, https://digitaltmuseum.no/021018406088/aalesund-borgund-kirke), but they are historic and do not name a current spot, so I did not use them. Visits to the church should be arranged in advance through the church office, per https://www.fjordnorway.com/en/see-and-do/borgund-church, because of services and funerals. Re-search with a local Ålesund photo guide if you need spots.
